input.question: How did the American Southern accent develop?
input.ground_truth: It's more the other way around, and relates to the question "When did American English break from British English?". At first American and British English were the same, but then British English developed into what it is today. American English has not changed as much, and is actually closer to British English of 200 years ago. American Southern has been even slower to change (because of the relative isolation of the speakers), and is even closer to British English of that time!

Question: How did the American Southern accent develop?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a big box of crayons, and some crayons are a little different from others because they’ve been in the sun or drawn on a lot. Now, let’s say you and your friends all start coloring with those crayons, but you all live in different parts of the playground. Over time, you all use the crayons a little differently. Some of you color the lines wavy, some straight, some use more red, some use more yellow.

The American Southern accent is a bit like that. Long ago, people who spoke English moved to the southern part of the United States. They all talked a little bit like each other at first, but as they lived in different places and met new people, their way of talking changed a little bit each time—kind of like how your crayon drawings might look a little different from your friend’s. Over many, many years, these small changes added up, and now people in the South sound a little different when they talk compared to people in other parts of the country. That’s how the Southern accent developed!
